title: Your First Spring Boot Project
summary: See what Spring Boot and Java are good at, install the tools, generate Roombook's project, answer your first request, and learn how Tomcat's threads serve many.
intro: The first two lessons looked at APIs from the outside: requests, responses, and the styles they come in. Now you build one. Before Roombook can answer a single request, you need the right tools on your computer, a project that anyone on your team can build the same way, folders with room to grow, and a server that starts with one command and picks up your changes. You'll repeat this setup at the start of every project, and when it's wrong, nothing after it works. This lesson covers what Spring Boot and Java are good at, installing them, generating the project, what each file is for, your first endpoint answering curl, and how Spring Boot serves many people at once with threads.

steps.title: What Spring Boot and Java are good for
steps.body:
Every API is built on a **stack**: a language, the program that runs it, and a framework on top. Knowing what yours does well tells you which jobs it suits, and which problems you'll have to plan around. This course's stack is Java, run by the JVM, with Spring Boot on top.

## Java runs on the JVM

You know Java from your language course. Its compiler, `javac`, doesn't turn your code into instructions for your processor. It turns it into **bytecode**, instructions for the **JVM**, the Java Virtual Machine, a program that runs bytecode on any computer. The JVM is Java's **runtime**, the program that runs code written in a language, and it's why the same compiled code runs on a Mac, on Windows, and on a Linux server. The last part of this lesson looks at what the JVM does while your API runs.

## Spring and Spring Boot

Java can already answer HTTP requests with the small server built into the JDK, but you'd do a lot by hand: check the method and the path of every request, write JSON yourself, set the headers, and handle errors. The first example below shows what that takes for a single route.

**Spring** does that work for you. Recall from the web course that you call a library, and a framework calls you. The **Spring Framework**, first released in 2003, is a large framework, and its part for HTTP is called **Spring MVC**. You write a method and mark it with an **annotation**, a label like `@GetMapping("/healthz")` that the Java course showed on methods like `@Override`. Spring reads the labels when the app starts and calls your method whenever a matching request arrives. That method is a **handler**, and a method and a path that lead to one handler make a **route**.

Setting up Spring by hand once took pages of configuration. **Spring Boot**, from 2014, does it for you, in three ways:

- **Starters**: one dependency that brings a whole set of libraries that work together. `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` brings Spring MVC, a web server, and Jackson, the library that turns Java objects into JSON.
- **Auto-configuration**: when the app starts, Spring Boot looks at which libraries are present and sets each one up with sensible defaults. It finds a web server, so it starts one, on port 8080.
- **An embedded server**: the web server, **Tomcat**, runs inside your app, so the app is one program you start with one command.

Spring Boot 4, from late 2025, is the current major version, on Spring Framework 7, and this course teaches its 4.2 release.

## What this stack is good at

- **Big systems that live for years.** Banks, airlines, and online shops run on Spring, with many teams working on the same code. Java's types and its editors make large changes safe: rename a method, and every use of it changes with it.
- **A library for everything.** Spring has its own projects for logins and permissions, databases, batch jobs, and messaging, all built to work together, plus every Java library ever written.
- **Speed once it's warm.** The JVM watches your code run and compiles the busiest parts to fast machine code, so a long-running server gets quicker over its first minutes.
- **Many requests at once, on many cores.** Java runs threads in parallel, and the last part of this lesson shows how that serves many requests.

## Where it's weak

- **Memory and startup.** A Spring Boot API uses a few hundred megabytes of memory and takes a second or more to start, more than a Go or Node.js server. That matters for tiny, short-lived jobs, and much less for an API that runs all day.
- **Magic.** Annotations and auto-configuration do a lot you never see. When something goes wrong, you need to know what Spring did on your behalf, so this course explains each piece as it appears.

## Its neighbors

You'll hear about other Java frameworks. **Quarkus** and **Micronaut** start faster and use less memory by doing more work when the code is compiled. **Javalin** is tiny, and close to the built-in server. The ideas in this course carry over to all of them, since they answer the same HTTP requests in much the same way.

examples.title: One route with only the JDK
examples.prompt: The HTTP server that comes with the JDK, answering `GET /healthz` with a little JSON. You don't need to save this: it's here to show what a framework takes off your hands.
examples.explanation: `createContext` sends every request whose path starts with `/healthz` to the function, so `/healthzzz` lands there too, a surprise you'd have to guard against. The function checks the method itself, writes the JSON as text with every quote escaped, counts the body's bytes for the status line call, and sets each header by hand. A second route is another `createContext`. A route like `/v1/rooms/3` means cutting the 3 out of the path yourself. Real APIs have dozens of routes, so this grows long and easy to get wrong.

examples.title: The same route with Spring Boot
examples.prompt: The same endpoint as a Spring controller. Spring Boot starts the server, so this class is all you write.
examples.explanation: `@RestController` marks a class whose methods answer requests, and whose return values become the response's body. `@GetMapping("/healthz")` adds a route: the method GET, the path `/healthz` exactly, and this method as its handler. The method returns an ordinary Java `Map`, and Jackson turns it into JSON and sets `Content-Type` for you. Spring answers 404 by itself for paths with no route, and 405 for a path whose method doesn't match. Each new route is one more annotated method. The rest of this lesson builds Roombook's real version of this class.

steps.title: Installing Java and your editor
steps.body:
Everything in this course runs on your own computer, in the Playground's terminal, so the first job is having the right tools there. Versions matter more than they look: a project written for one version of Java can fail to build on an older one with errors that never mention the version, and a team loses an afternoon finding out why.

## A JDK

To build and run Java, you need a **JDK**, a Java Development Kit: the compiler, `javac`, plus the JVM and Java's standard library. Several organizations build the same JDK from the same open source code. **Eclipse Temurin**, from the Adoptium project, is free, well tested, and a common choice for servers.

This course needs **Java 25 or newer**. Spring Boot 4 itself runs on Java 17 and up, but Roombook uses features from recent versions, like the virtual threads in the last part.

## LTS versions

Java puts out a new version every six months, and every two years one becomes **LTS**, short for Long Term Support: it gets bug and security fixes for years, so servers run one. Java 21 and Java 25 are LTS versions, and 25, from September 2025, is the newest.

## Installing it with SDKMAN

On a Mac or Linux, **SDKMAN** is a version manager for Java: it installs several JDKs side by side and switches between them per project, since sooner or later two projects will need two versions. Install it, then the JDK, with:

```bash
curl -s "https://get.sdkman.io" | bash
sdk install java 25-tem
```

The first command downloads SDKMAN's installer and runs it, and then you open a new terminal so it takes effect. The second installs Java 25 from Temurin, which is what `-tem` stands for, and makes it the default. On Windows, download the installer from [adoptium.net](https://adoptium.net) instead. Then check that it works with the commands in the example below.

## Maven comes with the project

Java projects are built with a **build tool**, a program that downloads the libraries a project needs, compiles the code, runs the tests, and packs the result. Roombook uses **Maven**, the most common one. You don't install it: every project brings a small script, the **Maven wrapper**, that downloads the right version of Maven the first time you use it, as the next part shows. The first build needs an internet connection for that.

## The terminal commands you'll use

The web course had you type a few commands. These are the ones every lesson from here on uses:

- `pwd` prints the folder the terminal is in, its **working directory**.
- `ls` lists what's in that folder.
- `mkdir roombook` makes a folder named roombook.
- `cd roombook` moves into it, and `cd ..` moves back up one level.
- **Ctrl+C** stops the program running in the terminal, like a server.
- The **Up arrow** brings back the last command, so you can run it again.

They work the same on a Mac and on Linux, and Windows PowerShell understands them too. Where a command differs on Windows, the lesson says so.

## Your editor

You can write the code in the Playground's editor, or in any editor you like. **IntelliJ IDEA** is the most common choice for Java and Spring: its free Community Edition understands Java fully, underlines mistakes as you type, and can rename a method everywhere it's used. **VS Code** works well too, with Microsoft's Extension Pack for Java and the Spring Boot Extension Pack. Either way, the editor can compile your code as you save, which the dev server in part 5 relies on.

examples.title: Checking the versions
examples.prompt: Type these in the Playground's terminal, one at a time. Notice the single dash in `-version`, an old Java habit.
examples.output:
openjdk version "25.0.2" 2026-01-20 LTS
OpenJDK Runtime Environment Temurin-25.0.2+10 (build 25.0.2+10-LTS)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM Temurin-25.0.2+10 (build 25.0.2+10-LTS, mixed mode, sharing)

examples.explanation: The first three lines come from `java`, the JVM. Its version is 25.0.2, an LTS release, built by Temurin. The three numbers are the feature release, then two levels of fixes. The third line names the JVM itself: a 64-bit server VM, in mixed mode, which means it interprets bytecode at first and compiles the busy parts as it runs. The last line is the compiler's version, which must match. Yours will likely be higher, and that's fine, as long as the first number is 25 or more.

steps.title: Generating the project
steps.body:
A **project** is a folder of code plus a file that lists everything the code needs. With that list, anyone can rebuild the project on any computer with one command and get the same versions you have. Getting it right on day one is what saves a team from the oldest excuse in software: it works on my machine.

## Spring Initializr

Nobody writes a Spring Boot project's starting files by hand. **Spring Initializr**, at [start.spring.io](https://start.spring.io), generates them: you pick the options on the website and download a zip file. It also answers curl, so in the Playground's terminal you can get exactly Roombook's project:

```bash
curl https://start.spring.io/starter.zip \
  -d type=maven-project \
  -d javaVersion=25 \
  -d groupId=dev.hackuniversity \
  -d artifactId=roombook \
  -d dependencies=web,actuator,devtools \
  -d configurationFileFormat=yaml \
  -d baseDir=roombook \
  -o roombook.zip
```

The backslash at the end of each line continues the command on the next. Each `-d` is one option:

- `type=maven-project` builds with Maven, and `javaVersion=25` targets Java 25.
- `groupId` and `artifactId` name the project: the group is usually your organization's domain, backwards, and the artifact is the project itself.
- `dependencies` picks the starters: `web` for Spring MVC and Tomcat, `actuator` for ready-made health checks, and `devtools` for restarts while you work. Later lessons add more, like database access and security, since each would get in the way of a first project: security, for one, locks every endpoint until there's a login.
- `configurationFileFormat=yaml` writes settings in YAML, and `baseDir=roombook` puts everything in a folder named roombook.

Then unpack it and move in, as the first example shows:

```bash
unzip roombook.zip
cd roombook
```

## pom.xml

`pom.xml` is Maven's project file, Java's version of the `package.json` you met in the web course. POM stands for Project Object Model, and the file is **XML**, a format of nested tags like HTML. The second example shows its key parts:

- The **parent**, `spring-boot-starter-parent`, version 4.2.0, sets the version of hundreds of libraries at once, all tested together. That's why the dependencies below it name no versions.
- `java.version` says which Java the code is compiled for.
- The **dependencies** are the starters you picked, plus two test starters. DevTools is marked `runtime` and `optional`, so it's used while you work and left out of the app you ship.
- The **plugin** teaches Maven Spring Boot's own commands, like `spring-boot:run`.

## No lockfile, on purpose

npm needs a lockfile because `package.json` allows ranges of versions. A `pom.xml` names exact versions, and the parent pins every library's version, so the same `pom.xml` gives the same libraries on every computer. Keep it that way: never write a version range in a `pom.xml`. Maven downloads the libraries into a **local repository**, a folder in your home directory, `~/.m2/repository`, shared by every project on your computer. So, unlike `node_modules`, nothing big lands in the project folder.

## The Maven wrapper

`mvnw`, and `mvnw.cmd` for Windows, is the **Maven wrapper**. `.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties` names the exact Maven version the project uses, 3.10.1 here, and the first time you run `./mvnw`, it downloads that version into `~/.m2/wrapper`. Every developer and every build server runs the same Maven, and nobody installs it by hand. The `./` in front means the `mvnw` file in this folder. In Windows PowerShell, type `.\mvnw` instead.

## Maven's commands

You'll use four, all from the project's folder:

- `./mvnw spring-boot:run` compiles the code and runs the server, as part 5 shows.
- `./mvnw compile` compiles the code into `target/classes`.
- `./mvnw test` compiles and runs the tests.
- `./mvnw package` builds `target/roombook-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar`, the whole app in one file, which `java -jar` runs. The deployment lesson ships it.

The first command downloads Maven and every library, which takes a minute. After that, everything comes from your local repository, and a build takes seconds.

A `test` scope means the library is only there while tests run, like npm's devDependencies. `0.0.1-SNAPSHOT` is Roombook's own version, and SNAPSHOT means still in development. steps.title: The project's files and folders
steps.body:
Where code lives decides how fast you can find it and how safely you can change it. A good layout puts each feature's code together, so a change to bookings happens in one place, and a Spring project's layout matters even more than most, because Spring finds your classes by where they are. Roombook starts small, but its layout is planned for everything the course adds.

```diagram first-project-tree
Today the project holds Maven's files, the entry point, and one controller. Each later lesson adds a package or two.
```

## Packages are folders

A **package** groups classes under one name, like `dev.hackuniversity.roombook`, and it's the group that package-private access, from your Java course, is about. Each part of the name is a folder: `src/main/java/dev/hackuniversity/roombook/`. Starting the name with a domain you own, written backwards, keeps your class names from ever clashing with a library's. Everything Roombook writes lives in this package, or in packages inside it.

## RoombookApplication.java

The **entry point**, the class you start, is the one Initializr wrote:

```java
@SpringBootApplication
public class RoombookApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(RoombookApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

`main` hands control to Spring, and `@SpringBootApplication` switches on three things: auto-configuration, settings written as code in this class, and **component scanning**. Scanning searches the class's package, and every package inside it, for classes marked with annotations like `@RestController`, `@Service`, and `@Repository`. Spring makes one object of each class it finds, called a **bean**, and hands each bean the other beans it needs. That's called dependency injection, and the lesson on layers explains it.

Here's the trap: scanning only looks inside `dev.hackuniversity.roombook`. A controller you put in `dev.hackuniversity.health`, one level up, is never found. Spring gives no warning, and every request to it gets a 404. Keep every class under the package that holds `RoombookApplication`.

## Packages by feature

As Roombook grows, each feature gets its own package inside the root one: `rooms`, `bookings`, `auth` for logins, and `feedback`. Each holds everything about its feature: the controller with its routes, the classes for its rules and its data that the lesson on layers introduces, and small **records**, Java's short way to write a class that only holds data, for the JSON that comes in and goes out. Some projects group code by kind instead, with one `controller` package, one `service` package, and so on. That splits every feature across many packages, so one change touches all of them. Grouping by feature keeps a change in one place.

Two packages hold what features share. `config` holds configuration classes, like the security setup in the lesson on logins, and `common` holds pieces every route uses, like the error handling that later lessons build. Roombook's health check gets a small package of its own, `health`.

## Resources and tests

`src/main/resources` holds files that aren't Java but ship with the app. `application.yaml` holds Roombook's settings, and later `db/migration` holds the files that build the database, from the lesson on raw SQL onward.

`src/test/java` mirrors the same packages, for the tests. Initializr wrote one already, `RoombookApplicationTests`, which checks that the app starts, and `./mvnw test` runs it.

## Settings and the environment

A setting that changes between computers, like the port or a database password, doesn't belong in the code. It goes in an **environment variable**, a named value the operating system hands a program when it starts. Spring Boot reads them for you, and maps names: an environment variable `SERVER_PORT` sets the setting `server.port`, capital letters and underscores for dots. That's called **relaxed binding**. `application.yaml` can also name a variable to use, with a default, as part 5 shows.

## What Git leaves out

Initializr wrote a `.gitignore`, the list of what Git, the tool that records versions of your code, should leave out. Its most important line is `target/`, the folder where Maven puts compiled classes and the packaged jar: anyone can rebuild it with `./mvnw package`. The rest covers the settings folders of the common editors, like `.idea` for IntelliJ.

examples.title: Roombook's application.yaml
examples.prompt: Replace `src/main/resources/application.yaml` with this. Initializr's version had only the first three lines.
examples.explanation: YAML nests settings by indenting them with spaces, never tabs, so `server.port` is written as `port` under `server`. `${PORT:8080}` means the environment variable `PORT` if it's set, and 8080 if it isn't, so the same file works on your computer and on a server that hands the app its port. Recall from the web course that `127.0.0.1` is loopback: only programs on your own computer can connect, which is what you want while you build. When Roombook runs on a real server, in the deployment lesson, `HOST` is set to `0.0.0.0` so other machines can reach it. `spring.application.name` names the app in its logs.

steps.title: Your first endpoint: GET /healthz
steps.body:
Nearly every API has one route that only answers: yes, I'm up. The tools that run your API in production, like the load balancers in the lesson on scaling out, call it every few seconds, and stop sending traffic to a copy that doesn't answer. It's also the simplest route there is, so it proves the whole setup works before you write anything real. Roombook's is `GET /healthz`. The z is a habit from Google's servers, and it makes the path unlikely to clash with a real resource.

## HealthController.java

Create `src/main/java/dev/hackuniversity/roombook/health/HealthController.java`:

```java
package dev.hackuniversity.roombook.health;

import java.util.Map;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
public class HealthController {

    @GetMapping("/healthz")
    public Map<String, String> health() {
        return Map.of("status", "ok");
    }
}
```

It's in `dev.hackuniversity.roombook.health`, inside the root package, so component scanning finds it. `@RestController` makes it a bean whose methods answer requests, and `@GetMapping` adds the route. The next lesson covers routes in full.

## Run it

Start the server in the Playground's terminal:

```bash
./mvnw spring-boot:run
```

Maven compiles the code and starts the app, and Spring Boot prints its banner, then log lines. Two say what you need: `Tomcat started on port 8080 (http) with context path '/'`, and `Started RoombookApplication in 0.8 seconds`. One early line also names your user account, the app's process id, and its folder, so check before you paste logs into a public chat. The server holds the terminal until you press Ctrl+C.

Many Spring guides use port 8080, which is Tomcat's default too, and it stays clear of Hack University, which uses 3000 on your computer. To run on another port for a moment, set the variable in front of the command:

```bash
PORT=9090 ./mvnw spring-boot:run
```

In Windows PowerShell, write `$env:PORT=9090; .\mvnw spring-boot:run` instead. If something already listens on the port, often an earlier copy of the server in another terminal, Spring stops at once with `APPLICATION FAILED TO START` and the reason: `Web server failed to start. Port 8080 was already in use.` Stop the other one with Ctrl+C, or pick another port.

## Restarts with DevTools

DevTools restarts the app whenever its compiled classes change, in about a tenth of a second, since it reloads only your own classes. Saving a `.java` file isn't enough on its own: the file has to be compiled first. Either run `./mvnw compile` in a second terminal after you save, or let your editor do it: in IntelliJ, turn on Build project automatically in its settings, and other editors have a setting like it. A restart throws away everything the server kept in memory, which is one reason real data goes in a database.

## Ask it with curl

The Playground's terminal is busy running the server, so send requests from a second one: your computer's own terminal, as in the web course, like Terminal on a Mac. The first example sends the request.

Next to your `/healthz`, the Actuator starter adds its own health check at `/actuator/health`, the second example. It reports UP or DOWN, and as Roombook gains a database, it checks that too, which the deployment lesson uses. Roombook keeps both: `/healthz` is the simple answer every course's Roombook gives, and the Actuator's is the detailed one.

Then ask for a path Roombook doesn't have yet:

```bash
curl -i http://localhost:8080/v1/rooms
```

Spring Boot answers `404` with JSON: a `timestamp`, the `status`, `Not Found`, a `message`, the `path`, and a very long `trace`, the list of Java methods that led to the error. The trace is there because DevTools turns it on while you develop. It's never in the app you ship, and the next lesson turns it off.

## Let the compiler check

Java checks your types when it compiles, before the server ever runs. Misspell `Map.of` as `Map.off` and save: `./mvnw compile` stops with `BUILD FAILURE` and an error naming the file, the line and column, `[13,19]`, then `cannot find symbol` and the missing `method off`. Watch the server too: the failed build deleted the old `HealthController` class, DevTools restarted without it, and `/healthz` now answers 404. Fix the typo and compile again, and it's back. `./mvnw test` goes further: it compiles, then runs the tests, and ends with `BUILD SUCCESS` when they pass. Run it before you commit, and the testing lesson makes the automated builds run it too.

examples.title: Calling GET /healthz
examples.prompt: From your computer's own terminal, with the server running in the Playground. `-i` makes curl print the response's status line and headers before the body.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 15
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:36:54 GMT

{"status":"ok"}
examples.explanation: The status is `200`, with no words after the number: Tomcat leaves out the reason phrase, since only the number counts. Jackson turned the `Map` into JSON, and Spring set `Content-Type` and `Content-Length`, the body's 15 bytes. There's no `Connection` header, because HTTP/1.1 keeps a connection open for the next request unless someone says otherwise, recall from the web course why that saves time. Spring adds nothing you didn't ask for, which keeps answers small.

examples.title: The Actuator's health check
examples.prompt: The same server, asked for the health endpoint that the Actuator starter added.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: application/vnd.spring-boot.actuator.v3+json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:36:54 GMT

{"groups":["liveness","readiness"],"status":"UP"}
examples.explanation: `status` is `UP`, the Actuator's word for healthy. `groups` lists two narrower checks it also offers, liveness, is the app running at all, and readiness, can it take traffic now, which the deployment lesson explains and uses. The `Content-Type` is the Actuator's own JSON type, version 3 of its format. `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` means the body is sent in pieces, each with its own length, in place of a `Content-Length` up front. You wrote none of this: auto-configuration saw the Actuator on the classpath and set it up.

steps.title: How Spring Boot handles many requests
steps.body:
Roombook will have hundreds of students checking rooms at the same moment. How a runtime serves many requests at once decides how fast your API is under load, and which mistakes slow everyone down. Spring Boot's answer starts with the JVM, and then with threads: one per request.

## What the JVM does while you run

The JVM starts by interpreting your bytecode, one instruction at a time. It counts how often each method runs, and compiles the busiest ones to machine code for your processor, which runs far faster. That's the **JIT**, the just-in-time compiler, and it's why a Java server is slower for its first few thousand requests and quick after that. The JVM also runs a **garbage collector**, or GC, which finds objects your code no longer uses and frees their memory, so you never free memory yourself. Both need memory to work in, which is part of why a Spring app uses hundreds of megabytes.

## Processes and threads

A **process** is a running program with its own memory: `./mvnw spring-boot:run` starts one. A **thread** is one line of work inside a process, running one instruction after another. A process can have many threads, and a computer has several **cores**, the parts of its processor that each run one thread at a time, so several threads can truly run at once. Java's ordinary threads, the ones `new Thread(...)` starts, are the operating system's own, called **platform threads**.

## One thread per request

Tomcat keeps a **thread pool**, a set of threads made once and reused, 200 by default. Each request that arrives borrows one, which runs your handler from start to finish and goes back to the pool when the response is sent.

```diagram first-project-runtime
On the left, each request holds a platform thread, even while it waits. On the right, a waiting virtual thread steps aside.
```

Follow the steps in the diagram:

1. A request arrives, and Tomcat hands it a thread of its own.
2. The handler asks the database for rooms. JDBC, Java's standard way to talk to databases, which the lesson on raw SQL uses, makes the thread wait for the answer, called **blocking**. A blocked thread does nothing else.
3. With 200 threads blocked, request 201 waits in line, even a health check that would take a microsecond.

So the number of threads caps how many requests can wait at once. Platform threads are costly: each reserves memory for its stack, and the operating system has to juggle them, so a server can't simply have 100,000 of them.

## Virtual threads

Java 21 added **virtual threads**: threads the JVM manages itself, so cheap that each request can have a new one. A few platform threads, called **carriers**, usually one per core, run them. Step 4 is the trick: when a virtual thread blocks, waiting on the database, the JVM takes it off its carrier and parks it in memory, a few kilobytes, and the carrier runs another one. When the answer arrives, the virtual thread gets back on a carrier and carries on.

Your code doesn't change. Blocking calls stay simple, one line after another, and the waiting costs almost nothing. Turn them on in `application.yaml`:

```yaml
spring:
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true
```

Tomcat then runs each request on a new virtual thread. Two catches remain. Virtual threads help with waiting, not computing: a request that computes for two seconds still holds its carrier for two seconds. And the limit moves elsewhere, usually to the number of database connections, which the lesson on databases at scale sizes. Before Java 24, a virtual thread blocked inside a `synchronized` block couldn't leave its carrier. Since Java 24 it can, one more reason to use Java 25.

## Shared beans, many threads

Every request runs on its own thread, but there's only one of each bean, so many threads run the same controller object at once. Never keep data about one request in a field of a bean: another request's thread can overwrite it mid-request. Keep per-request values in local variables, and when a bean must hold shared data, like the in-memory rooms of the next lesson, use classes built for many threads, like `ConcurrentHashMap`.

examples.title: A route that blocks
examples.prompt: A demo, not part of Roombook: `src/main/java/dev/hackuniversity/roombook/demo/SlowController.java`. It sleeps for two seconds, the way a thread waits on a slow database.
examples.explanation: `Thread.sleep` blocks the thread for two seconds, exactly what a blocking database call does to it: the thread can't serve anyone else meanwhile. To see the effect without sending 200 requests, the next examples start the server with a pool of only two threads. `SERVER_TOMCAT_THREADS_MAX=2` sets `server.tomcat.threads.max` through relaxed binding, just for that run. Delete the demo package when you're done, since it isn't part of Roombook.

examples.title: Two threads, both blocked
examples.prompt: Start the server with `SERVER_TOMCAT_THREADS_MAX=2 ./mvnw spring-boot:run`. Then, in your computer's own terminal, start two slow requests in the background, and time a health check behind them.
examples.code:
(curl -s localhost:8080/slow > /dev/null &)
(curl -s localhost:8080/slow > /dev/null &)
sleep 0.2
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "healthz answered in %{time_total}s\n" localhost:8080/healthz
examples.explanation: The `&` runs each slow curl in the background, and the parentheses keep the terminal from printing a note about it. `-w` prints how long the health check took, and `-o /dev/null` hides its body. Both of Tomcat's threads were asleep inside `/slow`, so the health check waited in line until one came back: 1.8 seconds, two seconds minus the head start. On a real server, the same thing happens with 200 threads and 200 slow queries.

examples.title: The same, on virtual threads
examples.prompt: Stop the server and start it again with virtual threads, keeping the pool of two: `SPRING_THREADS_VIRTUAL_ENABLED=true SERVER_TOMCAT_THREADS_MAX=2 ./mvnw spring-boot:run`. Then run the same three curl lines.
examples.code:
(curl -s localhost:8080/slow > /dev/null &)
(curl -s localhost:8080/slow > /dev/null &)
sleep 0.2
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "healthz answered in %{time_total}s\n" localhost:8080/healthz
examples.explanation: Under 20 milliseconds, most of it the first request's setup. Each request ran on a new virtual thread, so the two sleeping ones parked in memory and freed their carriers, and the health check never waited. The pool size no longer mattered, since Tomcat doesn't use its pool with virtual threads. The code didn't change at all: one setting moved the waiting off the threads. That's why many teams turn virtual threads on for APIs that spend their time waiting on databases and other services. The next lesson gives Roombook its real routes, for rooms and bookings.

recap:
- Java compiles to bytecode for the JVM, Spring MVC calls your annotated handlers, and Spring Boot adds starters, auto-configuration, and Tomcat.
- The stack shines at big, long-lived systems, and costs more memory and startup time than lighter ones.
- Spring Initializr generates the project, pom.xml names exact versions through its parent, and ./mvnw downloads Maven itself.
- Component scanning finds classes only in the main class's package and below, so keep every class under it.
- application.yaml reads PORT and HOST from the environment, with defaults of 8080 and 127.0.0.1.
- DevTools restarts the app when compiled classes change, so compile after saving, and ./mvnw test runs the checks.
- Tomcat gives each request a thread, and a blocked thread serves no one else until it returns.
- Virtual threads step aside while they wait, so waiting costs almost nothing, but computing still holds a carrier.
